title: You are that: the four great sayings
hookLine: a father hides salt in water and tells his son: you are that
carry: your self is not apart from brahman
tomorrow: the gods turn down a cow and a horse. why?

cards: A young man comes home after twelve years of study, a little proud of himself. His father, Uddalaka, asks a strange favor: put this salt in water, and bring it back in the morning. By morning the salt has vanished.
Taste it from the top, says the father. Salty. From the middle?
It's there, though you can't see it, he says. That fine essence is the self of everything. And you are that.

teach.b: Tat tvam asi, you are that, from the Chandogya Upanishad, is one of four very short lines that tradition gathers from four Upanishads and calls the mahavakyas, the great sayings.
The others: prajnanam brahma, consciousness is Brahman, from the Aitareya. Aham brahmasmi, I am Brahman, from the Brihadaranyaka. Ayam atma brahma, this self is Brahman, from the Mandukya.
Listen to the grammar: consciousness, I, you, this self.
Four doors to one Hindu teaching: the atman, your deepest self, is not apart from Brahman, the one reality. How is it read? In Advaita, Shankara's school, the self and Brahman are not two.

teach.h: NOT TWO, OR AN INNER RULER.
teach.b: For Ramanuja, the self is real and distinct, and Brahman dwells within it as its inner ruler, never apart. This lesson doesn't choose.
Many teachers hear the same idea in an everyday greeting: namaste, a bow to the one in front of you, read as honoring the divine in them. Now a neighbor.
The Buddha's Dhammapada opens, in Max Müller's translation: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts."
Both send the seeker inward. The honest difference: the Buddha's teaching declines to name a lasting self, and doesn't point to Brahman. The great sayings name both.

how: Hindu teachers in the Vedanta schools study the four great sayings closely; Advaita reads them as pointing to the non-difference of self and Brahman, while Vishishtadvaita reads them as Brahman dwelling in the self as its inner ruler.

o: four great sayings that name the self and Brahman
four vows a monk takes on entering a monastery
four prayers said at the day's four temple rituals

games.q: four sayings, four homes. tap the pairs.
p: this self is Brahman: the Mandukya

s: tat tvam asi comes from the Chandogya Upanishad
where Uddalaka dissolves salt in water for his son.
every Vedanta school reads the sayings as 'self and Brahman are not two'
that's Advaita; for Ramanuja, Brahman dwells in a real, distinct self as its inner ruler.
the Dhammapada and the great sayings say the same thing about the self
both turn inward; the Buddha's teaching declines to name a lasting self or Brahman.

games.q: a Buddhist friend reads you the Dhammapada's first line and asks: so Hindus and Buddhists say the same thing about the self? what's the honest answer?
o: we share the turn inward; the Buddha doesn't name a lasting self or Brahman.
yes, exactly the same: both say the self is Brahman.
no, nothing shared: Buddhism isn't interested in the mind.
games.why: Both send the seeker inward to the mind. The great sayings name the self and Brahman; the Buddha's teaching declines to name a lasting self.

practice: Close your eyes, if that's comfortable. Let one of the four sayings rest in the mind, whichever comes: you are that, or I am Brahman. Don't work it out.
Let it sit like a stone in clear water, and notice the quiet knowing that notices it.

wordCard.voice: The four mahavakyas: four great sayings from four Upanishads, starting with prajnanam brahma, consciousness is Brahman.

orig.note: Sanskrit: mahavakya, a great saying; tradition gathers four of them from the Upanishads.

carryVoice: Keep this: your self is not apart from Brahman. Four great sayings, one old teaching. The great sayings, begun.

sources.ref: Aitareya Upanishad 3.1.3 (prajnanam brahma); Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.10 (aham brahmasmi); Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7 (tat tvam asi; Shvetaketu's return in 6.1 and the salt in water in 6.13); Mandukya Upanishad 2 (ayam atma brahma)
Advaita and Vishishtadvaita readings of the great sayings (Shankara; Ramanuja, Vedartha Sangraha and Sri Bhashya); namaste read as honoring the divine in the other (a common teachers' reading)

sources.q: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts.
